newsitem.title: LEBANON: Fear, uncertainty plague south Lebanon zone.
newsitem.headline: Fear, uncertainty plague south Lebanon zone.

text.p: Rockets and bombs grab the headlines but the real struggle for residents of south Lebanon caught in the war between Israel and Hizbollah guerrillas is economic survival.

Those on the last active Arab front line with Israel have been marginalised by war, domestic politics and the impasse in Middle East peace talks. They try to make ends meet in a region that is noticed only when there is a surge in violence, like the current battles.

"We live in exile," said Asaad, a Shi'ite farmer from Khiam village who lives in isolation from the rest of Lebanon. The father of five children exists on the $250 a month rent from a second house he owns in the village.
Out of 400,000 officially registered residents, only 130,000 remain in the zone.

A peace agreement is probably the only way to end Israel's 19-year presence in Lebanon, which it says is necessary to protect northern Israel. Israel's current occupation zone, carved out in 1985, is patrolled by its own troops and its client militia, the South Lebanon Army (SLA).
There are five crossing points into areas controlled by the Lebanese government. But fighting between Israel and Hizbollah (Party of God) spills onto both sides of the Israeli-Lebanese lines.
The lack of progress in the peace talks has deepened the anguish of residents. There have been no Israeli talks with Syria or Lebanon since early 1996.
"Fear rules here," said Nada, a 35-year-old housewife. "What if a child gets sick? We don't have anyone to turn to. We are literally on our own".
In April 1996 Israeli artillery bombarded south Lebanon for 17 straight days. Israeli gunners killed about 100 civilians sheltering at a U.N. peacekeeping base in the village of Qana.

A U.S.-brokered ceasefire ended the onslaught and banned Hizbollah and Israel from targetting civilians. That had cut the toll, but last week seven Lebanese civilians died in a three-day span from Israeli shells and bombs planted by unknown assailants.
A LAND OF CONFUSION
The zone is a confusion of entangled identities. Many people, who dance to Lebanese nationalist songs while sipping Israeli beer, fear they could still suffer after peace.
So far in 1997 Beirut's military court has imposed jail sentences on about 200 Lebanese in absentia -- mostly zone residents -- for collaborating and dealing with Israel.
Abou Ali, a 62-year-old contractor for infrastructure projects, says he is caught in the middle, forced to import asphalt and fuel from Israel by Israel's proxy militia.

"I work with the Lebanese government and the Israeli government. I can't leave either of them if I want to survive," he said. "What the world must understand is that we live under occupation. We are no less Lebanese than others."

Many other residents feel they also have no choice. The tranquil hills, streams and lush greenery in the 15-km (nine mile) wide zone belie a struggle for economic survival. Despite the potential, agriculture and industry are poorly developed.
"Everyday, Israeli fruits and vegetables enter from Israel. They sell at cheaper prices while the cost of production is prohibitively high here," Asaad said.
"We are not banned from taking our produce to Beirut or other Lebanese areas but paper work and delays at Lebanese army checkpoints have made it very difficult to do," he said.
Only a third of the Marjayoun plain is farmed, partly due to a shortage of water because the Lebanese government in 1996 stopped a project to dig irrigation canals.
Munir, a 45-year-old Shi'ite, said he shut his $250,000 factory producing detergents, shampoos and candles in 1993 when he failed to sell 50 percent of his production.
"To continue, I had to take 10 tonnes of products outside the zone every month. In recent years, we were being harassed at checkpoints. We accumulated stocks and debts," he said bitterly.
DESPERATION DRIVES MERCENARIES
Driven more by necessity than conviction, many Shi'ite and Christian men have joined the 3,000-strong SLA, which is led by General Antoine Lahd who is under a Lebanese death sentence for treason.

Yussef, 28, said he joined the SLA during Lebanon's civil war which ended in 1990: "I did not have many options then. Now, I paint houses so I left the army. Many of my friends are still there because they can't do anything else."
Israel pays SLA fighters an average monthly salary of $400, with the further enticement that some 2,000 relatives get to work in Israel for higher wages.
"As I am not a farmer, I had to choose between the SLA or trading," said Jean, who expects his expertise in selling Israeli goods will be in demand when there is peace and open borders.
Trading in Israeli products, especially food, flourished in the late 1980s when, according to Jean, the area was Lebanon's "garbage dump for expired goods".
Since then the Lebanese army has tightened its grip on the exits from the Israeli zone to secure Lebanese government-held areas and end the smuggling of Israeli goods.
"Now the government wants to blame me for what I do for living," said Jean. "What did it offer me instead?"
